messages.say: John deer x350 lawn tractor drain gas tank

For a John Deere X350, the key point (that trips people up) is this:

There is no dedicated drain plug on the fuel tank. (JustAnswer)

So you’re not going to find a bolt on the bottom to open. You have to remove the fuel another way.



Practical methods (X350-specific)


Method 1 - Disconnect fuel line (most direct)


This is the standard approach for that model.


Steps:


Park on level ground, engine off, cool.

Turn off fuel shutoff valve (if equipped).

Locate the fuel line (tank → fuel filter/carb).

Clamp or pinch the line (optional but cleaner).

Disconnect the line at the carburetor or filter.

Aim it into a gas can and let it drain.


This works because gravity will empty the tank through the line.

Expect a steady flow-have a container ready.


This is specifically recommended for X350 since there’s no drain port. (JustAnswer)



Method 2 - Siphon from the tank (simpler, less disassembly)


If you don’t want to mess with hoses:


Remove gas cap

Insert siphon pump hose

Pump fuel into approved container


This is the lowest-risk method for spills if you’re careful. (ToolingIdeas)



Method 3 - Run it dry (least precise)


Just run the mower until it stalls.

Still leaves a little fuel in the system.


This is fine for maintenance but not ideal if you’re trying to fully empty the tank.



Important cautions (don’t skip)


Work outside or with strong ventilation

No sparks, cigarettes, or hot engines

Use a proper gas can

Clean spills immediately


Gas fumes + small engines = real ignition risk.



Common mistakes (worth avoiding)


Pulling the fuel line without a container ready

Forgetting to shut off the fuel valve (if present)

Trying to tip the mower (bad idea-spills into engine)



Bottom line


X350 = no drain plug

Best method = disconnect fuel line or siphon

Siphon is cleaner; fuel-line method is more complete



If you want, I can walk you through exactly where the fuel line is on your X350 (it varies slightly by deck/engine config).



Sources:


How to Drain Fuel Tank on X350 Mower – Expert Guide - JustAnswer

How to Drain Gas from a John Deere Riding Lawn Mower?

You’ve actually got everything you need in those photos—and your instinct to use that siphon pump is the right move. I’ll be specific based on what I can see.



What I see (important)


The fuel line + inline filter (3rd image) is clearly accessible

Standard gravity-fed setup (no obvious electric pump inline there)

Your siphon pump kit is perfectly adequate for this job



Best option for your exact setup → Use the siphon (cleanest)


Given your access and that you already bought the tool, don’t overcomplicate this.


How to do it correctly


Remove the gas cap

Feed the clear hose into the tank
You may need to angle it slightly to get past the filler neck bend

Put the outlet hose into a gas can (lower than tank)

Squeeze the bulb repeatedly until flow starts

Let gravity finish the job


Key detail most people miss


The tank outlet is not at the absolute bottom, so you’ll likely leave a small amount (normal)



Alternative (more complete but messier)


If you want it fully drained, use what’s in your 3rd image:


Disconnect here:


The fuel line at the carb side of that inline filter


Then:


Stick that hose into a container

Fuel will gravity drain


Caveat


You’ll get more fuel out this way, but:


It’s messier

Those red clamps are annoying (you’ll likely cut/replace them)



What I would not do


Don’t try to siphon through that fuel line (too restrictive)

Don’t tip the mower (people do this—bad idea)

Don’t disconnect both sides of the filter unless you enjoy spills

One more practical note


Your fuel filter looks a bit discolored—nothing alarming, but if you’re already draining fuel, it’s a good time to replace it. They’re cheap and often overlooked.

Ah, that makes perfect sense. Sitting outside exposed to the elements all winter is tough on these machines.
Adding fresh fuel and treatment was a logical thought, but unfortunately, it doesn't cure the old gas—especially the gas that is already sitting at the front of the line. Over a long, freezing winter, ethanol-blended gas breaks down, turns to varnish, and pulls in moisture from the air.
Right now, the engine is trying to drink that old, watery gas sitting in the fuel line and the carburetor, which is why it won't fire up.
Here is how to attack this:


1. Evacuate the Tank


Go ahead and use that siphon pump you bought to get as much of that mixed fuel out of the tank as possible. You want to start with a completely clean slate.


2. Purge the Carburetor Bowl (Crucial Step)


This is the part most people miss. Even if you drain the tank, the carburetor is still full of the bad winter gas.


Look at the carburetor (at the end of the fuel line, past the filter).

At the very bottom of the carburetor, there is a small metal bowl.

There is a small bolt/screw at the base of that bowl. Put a rag under it and loosen that bolt. Let all the old gas dribble out until it stops, then tighten the bolt back up.


3. Check for Unwanted Winter Guests


Tractors sitting outside over the winter are prime real estate for field mice. I noticed some droppings on your dashboard in that third photo. Before you try starting it again, take a quick flashlight tour under the green hood and around the engine shroud. Make sure no mice have built nests in the cooling fins or chewed through any of your ignition wires.


4. Refill and Prime


Swap in that new fuel filter (since the old one is holding bad gas anyway), hook the lines back up, and add your two gallons of fresh, treated fuel. You may have to crank it for a few extra seconds to let the fuel pump push the new gas through the dry lines and into the carburetor.
To help narrow this down further if the fuel purge doesn't work: when you turn the key, is the engine actually cranking over rapidly (chug-chug-chug), or is it just clicking/spinning very slowly?

Most of what you wrote is directionally right, but a couple of points need tightening so you don’t chase the wrong failure mode.



What you’re getting right


Old ethanol fuel degradation → real issue (oxidation + phase separation)

Carb bowl still holding bad fuel → absolutely true, often overlooked

Mice risk → your photos do show droppings; that’s not speculative

Siphoning tank first → correct sequence


So the overall plan is solid. The weak spot is how strongly you’re attributing the no-start only to bad fuel.



Where I’d push back


1. “Old gas = won’t fire” is not always sufficient


Even degraded fuel will often still produce some ignition (rough sputter, partial firing). A total no-start can also be:


Low battery / weak cranking

Ignition issue (coil, plug, safety switch)

Carb jet blockage (not just bad fuel sitting there)


So don’t assume fuel is the only variable.



Tightened procedure (more precise)


Step 1 — Drain tank (what you said)


Use the siphon. Good.



Step 2 — Carb bowl drain (critical, but here’s the nuance)


You’re correct in principle, but:


Not all X350 carbs have an obvious “easy” drain bolt

Sometimes it’s actually the bowl retaining bolt itself


What to do:


Put a rag or container underneath

Loosen (not fully remove) the bottom-center bolt on the carb bowl

Let it drain completely


If nothing comes out → that’s actually diagnostic:


Could mean clogged inlet / stuck float



Step 3 — Fuel filter (your suggestion is reasonable)


But be precise:


That filter in your photo is partially filled and discolored

That’s not definitive failure, just aging


Replace it if:


You’re already disconnecting lines (low cost, low effort)



Step 4 — Prime and crank (important correction)


You said:

“fuel pump pushes new gas through”

On many X350s:


It’s a vacuum pulse pump, not electric

It only moves fuel while cranking


So:


Expect longer crank time (10–20 sec bursts)

Possibly multiple attempts



Step 5 — Mice inspection (this is not optional in your case)


You already have visible droppings.


Focus on:


Under engine shroud (cooling fins)

Around ignition coil wire

Air intake housing


A chewed ignition wire = perfect crank, zero spark



Fast diagnostic shortcut (before all this work)


Do this first—it saves time:


Spray a small shot of starter fluid into intake


Remove air filter

Spray briefly

Try to start


Interpret result:


Fires briefly → fuel system problem (your plan is correct)

No response → ignition/compression issue


This is a much cleaner diagnostic than assuming fuel.



Bottom line


Your plan is mostly correct, but slightly overconfident in a single cause.


Best sequence:


Quick starter fluid test (diagnostic)

Siphon tank

Drain carb bowl

Replace filter (optional but sensible)

Inspect for rodent damage

Refill + extended crank

If it’s cranking normally but not even trying to fire, you need to be careful here—you’re probably over-weighting the fuel hypothesis.


A pure fuel issue usually gives you some sputter or attempt to catch.
A true no-fire at all often points to ignition (spark) or safety interlocks, not just stale gas.



First: don’t guess — verify spark


Before buying parts, do this quick check:


Spark test (2 minutes)


Pull the spark plug wire off

Remove the spark plug

Reconnect plug to the wire

Hold metal threads against engine block

Crank engine


Result:


Visible blue spark → ignition is fine → go back to fuel

No spark → stop focusing on fuel



If you have NO spark (likely given your description)


1. Safety switch system (very common on Deere)


These will kill spark completely, even while cranking.


Check:


Seat switch (bounce on seat while cranking)

Brake pedal fully depressed

PTO switch OFF

Reverse safety (try neutral position)


👉 These fail all the time and mimic ignition failure.



2. Rodent damage (you already have evidence)


This is not hypothetical in your case.


Look closely for:


Chewed thin black wires near engine

Damage near ignition coil

Nesting under shroud


Even a single broken kill wire = no spark.



3. Ignition coil / kill wire test


This is the fastest isolation test and very telling.


Do this:


Locate the ignition coil (on engine, near flywheel)

There will be a small thin wire (kill wire) attached


👉 Disconnect that wire


Then crank:


Spark appears → problem is in wiring/safety switches

Still no spark → coil or magneto issue


This is a high-value test. Don’t skip it.



4. Spark plug (cheap, but not a primary suspect)


Replace it anyway:


~$5–10

Eliminates a variable


But realistically:

A bad plug alone rarely causes zero spark at the wire.


5. Battery voltage (subtle but real)


Even if it cranks:


Weak battery → low ignition output on some systems

Your dash showed ~12V-ish, which is borderline but not terrible


Still worth:


Charging battery fully before testing



Where fuel fits in now


You’re not wrong that:


Old gas + carb contamination is a problem


But based on:

“turns over, doesn’t fire at all”

Fuel is secondary until spark is confirmed.



Parts you might need (don’t buy yet)


Only after testing:


Spark plug (safe to buy now)

Fuel filter (since you’re already working there)

Ignition coil (only if confirmed no spark after kill wire test)

Possibly safety switch (if intermittent/no spark)



Clean diagnostic flow (don’t skip order)


Spark test

If no spark → disconnect coil kill wire

If still no spark → coil issue

If spark returns → wiring/safety switch issue

Only then go deep on fuel system



Bottom line


You’re probably dealing with ignition shutdown, not just bad gas.
The rodent evidence makes wiring damage a serious contender.

What “tries to start” usually means


This pattern is classic:


Engine catches for a second → dies

Repeats on crank

Maybe a weak sputter


That almost always indicates:

Fuel delivery / carb issue, not ignition


Immediate priority (to avoid killing the battery)


Don’t keep cranking blindly


Limit to 5–10 second bursts

Wait ~30 seconds between attempts


You’re right to worry—these small batteries drain fast.



Fastest path forward (minimal cranking)


1. Do a quick confirmation (very high value)


Before tearing into anything:


Spray test


Remove air filter

Spray a small amount of starter fluid (or even carb cleaner)

Crank


Result:


Fires briefly and dies → 100% fuel issue

No change → revisit spark/compression


This saves a lot of guesswork.



If it fires with spray → proceed


2. Use the siphon (you already have it)


Drain tank as planned



3. Drain carb bowl (this is likely your real problem)


What’s happening right now:


Old fuel sitting in carb bowl

That’s what the engine is pulling first


Action:


Loosen bottom bolt on carb bowl

Drain completely

Tighten back up



4. Replace that fuel filter (your photo)


I’d do it. It’s cheap and:


It’s holding old fuel

It adds restriction when dirty



5. Refill + prime (be patient)


After everything is dry:


Add fresh gas (treated is fine)

Crank in short bursts


Expect:


A few attempts before it fully runs

It may run rough for 30–60 seconds



If it STILL won’t run after that


Then you’re likely here:

Carburetor jet partially clogged (varnish)

Symptoms:


Starts only with spray

Dies immediately without it


Next step:


Carb clean (remove bowl + clean main jet)



Battery management (practical)


Since you're concerned (correctly):


If available, hook up a charger while working

Or jump from another battery (engine OFF on donor vehicle)



Bottom line


Given your updated symptom:


Spark is probably fine

Fuel system contamination is now the leading cause


Start with:


Spray test (confirm)

Drain tank

Drain carb bowl

Replace filter

Retry



If it fires on spray but won’t stay running, I can walk you through exactly how to clean that carb on your engine—it’s not as bad as it sounds.
Hose won’t come off

Yeah—that’s the classic Deere setup with factory spring clamps (those red clips). They’re doing their job… maybe too well.


You’re not doing anything wrong—those hoses can be very stubborn, especially after sitting.



What’s happening


The hose has essentially bonded itself to the barb (heat + age + fuel residue)

Just pulling won’t work and can tear the hose



Correct way to get it off (don’t brute force)


Step 1 — Move the clamp (you already did this)


Good—you’ve slid the red clamp back. That part is fine.



Step 2 — Break the seal (this is the key step)


Before pulling, you need to twist, not yank.


Grab hose close to the fitting

Rotate it back and forth

Even a tiny movement breaks the seal


👉 If it won’t twist, that’s normal—go to next step.



Step 3 — Use a pick or small flat screwdriver


Carefully:


Slide a small flathead or pick between hose and metal barb

Gently pry just enough to let air in


⚠️ Don’t gouge the barb or slice the hose



Step 4 — Then pull while twisting


Once it moves even slightly:


Twist + pull at the same time

It should come off



If it’s still stuck (common)


Option A — Heat it slightly


Use a hair dryer or heat gun (low)

Warm the hose for ~20–30 seconds


This softens it and makes removal much easier.



Option B — Cut it (honestly often the smartest move)


Given:


That hose looks aged

You already have it apart


👉 Just slice it lengthwise and peel it off


Then replace with:


1/4" fuel line (likely size, but match it)

Standard worm clamp (easier next time)



Important observation from your photo


That filter:


Is full of dark/old fuel

Looks partially restricted


Even if you get the hose off:

I would replace both the filter and that short hose section


My recommendation (practical, not theoretical)


Don’t fight it for 20 minutes.


Cut the hose

Replace hose + filter

Reassemble clean


This is faster and more reliable than trying to “save” old fuel line.



Bottom line


You’re stuck because the hose is sealed to the barb—not clamped too tight

Twisting or breaking the seal is required

Cutting + replacing is often the better call on machines like this



If you want, I can tell you the exact hose size and a clean routing so you only have to do this once.
How many fuel lines are there? Aren't there two, one on either end of that filter? One is way easier to replace than the other.

Yes, you’re correct. There are indeed two lines—one coming from the tank to the inlet side of the filter, and another leading from the outlet side to the carburetor. In practice, the line going toward the carburetor is usually shorter and more accessible. Replacing that one is often easier, and it might suffice if you’re just doing maintenance. However, if the tank-side line is deteriorated or you’re dealing with old fuel throughout, it’s best to inspect both lines and replace them if they’re worn. It’s a good idea to replace both lines if one shows any sign of aging.

“Carburetor spray” usually means one of two aerosol products:


Carburetor cleaner

Starting fluid (ether spray)


They are related but used differently.



What you probably want right now


Since you’re diagnosing a no-start:


Best diagnostic tool:


Starting fluid


It’s specifically made to help engines fire briefly.


Common labels:


“Starting Fluid”

“Engine Starting Spray”


Usually:


Ether-based

In aerosol can



Carb cleaner vs starting fluid

Product
Purpose
Better for
Carb cleaner
Dissolves varnish/gunk
Cleaning carb
Starting fluid
Ignites very easily
Diagnosing fuel issues


What to do now


Step 1


Remove or open the air filter housing.


You want access to:


The carb intake/throttle body



Step 2


Spray a very short burst
About:


1 second max


Do NOT soak it.



Step 3


Immediately crank engine.


Interpret result:


If engine fires briefly:


That strongly confirms:


Spark exists

Compression probably fine

Fuel delivery/carb issue


If absolutely nothing changes:


Then:


Ignition/spark problem still possible

Or compression issue



Important caution


Do NOT repeatedly spray huge amounts.


Too much:


Washes cylinder walls

Can backfire

Hard on engine


Small burst only.

If it fires on spray:


Your next move is:


Drain tank

Drain carb bowl

Replace filter

Fresh fuel

Possibly clean carb jet


That becomes a very coherent diagnosis.



One more practical note


If you only have carb cleaner, you can use a tiny amount for testing in a pinch. It’s just less ideal and sometimes harder to ignite than true starting fluid.


So:


Starting fluid = preferred

Carb cleaner = acceptable fallback
both?

For your situation


You’re trying to answer:

“Is this fundamentally a fuel delivery problem?”

So:


Use starting fluid first


That gives the cleanest signal.



What success looks like


If you spray starting fluid and the engine:


coughs

sputters

runs for 1–2 seconds


…then your ignition system is probably fine and the engine just isn’t getting usable gasoline.


That would strongly support:


stale fuel

clogged carb jet

fuel delivery restriction



Then where carb cleaner fits


After diagnosis:


carb cleaner helps clean the carburetor internals

especially the main jet and bowl


But carb cleaner alone often won’t dissolve severe varnish without some disassembly.



If you’re at the store


You can honestly buy:


1 can starting fluid

1 can carb cleaner


They’re inexpensive and both useful for mower rehab.



One caution


Some modern engines dislike excessive ether use.


So:

don’t keep spraying repeatedly while cranking


You’re diagnosing, not trying to run the engine on ether indefinitely.

2. Drain the old fuel

People often say:

On your X350, the carburetor is behind the air filter housing on the side of the engine under the hood. You’re actually already very close to it in your earlier photos.


Easy orientation


In your photo with the fuel filter:


Fuel line goes:
tank → filter → carburetor

The carb is where that hose ends.



How to access it


1. Raise hood

2. Locate air filter box


Look for:
